newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African telecommunications bill set for adoption.
newsitem.headline: S.African telecommunications bill set for adoption.

text.p: Opposition parties abandoned a bid on Friday to delay what they called a flawed framework for partial privatisation of South Africa's Telkom utility, but businessmen threatened a court challenge.
Post Master General Andile Ngcaba told Reuters the Telecommunications Bill currently before parliament would establish a framework for the sale of up to 30 percent of Telkom.
The highly-prized stake is expected to go to an international investor for an estimated five to six billion rand ($1.1-1.3 billion) in cash, plus additional investment in technology and training.
"The bill facilitates a faster move to competition. This is a change to a much more competitive environment in which the marketplace will be clear on what are the rules," he said.
But the National Party, Freedom Front and Democratic Party say the bill is being rammed through parliament and that it will leave too much power in the hands of the government.

"It's all about competition, which this bill does not encourage," said Democratic Party Senator Errol Moorcroft, who criticised the exclusion of a limit on the state-owned Telkom utility's monopoly on traditional telephone services.
"If other players in the industry face an undetermined period of time before their case is put, they're going to say the hell with it and take their business elsewhere," he said.

The National Telecommunications Co-ordinating Group (NTCG) representing nine telecommunications associations, said in a letter to legislators that it would take legal advice on a constitutional challenge to aspects of the bill.
The NTCG said the bill, including amendments made by the National Assembly before its adoption there on Thursday, gave the Minister of Posts and Telecommunications too much power.
"The principle of free and fair competition is now being ignored," the group said.

Ngcaba said the government would honour the four-to-six year limit on exclusive Telkom operations in traditional telephony laid down in its policy white paper, adding: "We regard that as government policy."

But he said his department should have the freedom to use the range of exclusivity as a negotiating tool in talks with potential partners for Telkom and said the exclusivity period would be written into a licence agreement.
Ngcaba said the seven potential equity partners shortlisted by Posts and Telecommunications Minister Jay Naidoo last month were all happy with the bill before parliament.
"They are very comfortable, all of them. They are up to date, they've got people here and they have no reservations. The bill is fine as far as they are concerned," he said.
The firms shortlisted are Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom, KPN of the Netherlands, Telekom Malaysia, South Western Bell of the United States, Italy's Stet and Telia of Sweden.

The three opposition parties abandoned a bid to amend the bill before it is adopted by the Senate on Tuesday when the majority African National Congress made it clear they would not entertain significant amendments.
Ngcaba said the selection of a South African Telecommunications Regulatory Authority would begin as soon as President Nelson Mandela signs the bill into law, probably later this month.
He said the authority would be appointed before the end of the year, but Telkom's first licence to operate under the new law would be prepared by his department to avoid delays.
